slides.title: Measure a named boundary before comparing numbers
keyPoints: Latency has a start and completion event
Throughput counts useful completions per interval
CPU time and elapsed time answer different questions
slides.narration: A benchmark number has little meaning until we know what happened inside its boundary. A request's latency might include waiting in a queue, parsing, computation, and delivery, while a kernel benchmark may time only one prepared loop. Throughput counts completed useful work over an elapsed interval. CPU time counts processor execution under the operating system's accounting rules. These are not interchangeable units of success. This chapter uses both actual timing mechanics and explicitly supplied observations. When we calculate a model result, we will label it as such rather than pretending that deterministic output is a measurement of this machine.

slides.title: Concurrent request durations are not the elapsed interval
keyPoints: Three requests overlap from 0 to 10 milliseconds
Each latency is 10 milliseconds
Three completions in 10 milliseconds give 300 per second
slides.narration: Our supplied observations describe three requests that all begin at zero and complete at ten milliseconds. Adding their durations produces thirty milliseconds of request time, but the observed wall interval is only ten. Dividing three by that actual interval gives three hundred completions per second. The incorrect serial assumption gives one hundred. The program prints both calculations and labels the sum-based one wrong. These are arithmetic over a stated fixture, not timings collected by the program. This distinction matters whenever requests overlap: throughput needs a completion count and an elapsed observation window, not the sum of individual response durations.

slides.title: One average can hide very different users’ waits
keyPoints: Nine requests take 1 ms; one takes 91 ms
Mean is 10 ms while the median is 1 ms
Nearest-rank p95 is 91 ms for this small sample
slides.narration: This supplied sample has nine quick requests and one slow request. The total is one hundred milliseconds across ten observations, giving a mean of ten. After sorting, the lower central observation is one, and both middle observations are one, so the median is one. Under the nearest-rank percentile rule, the ninety-fifth percentile selects rank ten and is ninety-one. The output makes the long tail visible, but ten samples do not establish a reliable population tail estimate. A percentile needs a stated definition, sample count, and representative workload. Sorting a local vector is acceptable here because the fixture's original order is not needed later.

question.answer: No. It is the selected order statistic of this small fixture. Population inference needs enough representative measurements and uncertainty analysis.

slides.title: CPU seconds can exceed elapsed seconds
keyPoints: A process may execute on several cores
Waiting contributes wall time without equal CPU time
State whether accounting covers one thread or the whole job
slides.narration: A four-thread computation can use roughly four CPU seconds during one second of elapsed time if all four run continuously on separate cores. That is not a broken clock; CPU time adds execution charged across threads. Conversely, a job can take two wall seconds while using only six-tenths of a CPU second because it waits for I/O or scheduling. The difference suggests where to investigate, but does not identify one cause by itself. Helper processes and kernel accounting boundaries can also matter. Record whether your number covers one thread, one process, or the complete multi-process job.

question.prompt: Is process CPU time greater than wall time automatically invalid?
question.answer: No. Multiple threads can accumulate CPU execution simultaneously on different cores. The accounting scope must be stated.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: The mean describes total time divided by count; the selected percentile describes an order statistic. Sorting a copy preserves the caller’s sample order. Three observations make a very weak basis for real tail-latency inference: the example teaches the calculation, not statistical confidence. Throughput here uses a serial interval; concurrent request durations cannot simply be added to infer wall time.
A plausible alternative: A checksum or observable result keeps benchmark work relevant, but timing still needs warmup, repetitions, and controlled comparisons.

SOURCE TOPIC
Throughput measures completed useful work per unit time.
It can be expressed as records, requests, or bytes per second.
Define whether failed requests, retries, warmup work, and partial completions count.
Throughput and latency interact through queueing.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
LECTURE NARRATION
Throughput measures completed useful work per unit time. It can be expressed as records, requests, or bytes per second. Define whether failed requests, retries, warmup work, and partial completions count. Throughput and latency interact through queueing. A system can increase completed work by admitting more concurrent requests while making each request wait longer. Evaluate the service objective rather than maximizing a single number without constraints.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

slides.title: Utilization
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Utilization describes the fraction of a resource’s capacity in use under a stated definition.
CPU utilization, memory bandwidth utilization, and device busy time are different metrics.
High CPU utilization does not prove that useful work is progressing efficiently; a spin loop can consume an entire core.
Low utilization does not automatically mean spare end-to-end capacity.

slides.title: A clock read has cost and a limited resolution
keyPoints: Use a monotonic clock for durations
Very short work can be smaller than clock granularity
Batch enough work without silently changing the workload
slides.narration: Civil time can be adjusted, so duration measurements should normally use a monotonic clock such as steady_clock. Even that clock has a finite resolution and reading it has overhead. If one operation is extremely short, a measured zero does not imply infinite speed; it may be below the clock's visible scale. Batching operations can enlarge the interval, but also changes cache reuse and amortizes setup. State whether that batch represents the actual requirement. Keep the clock outside the operation only when the boundary excludes its overhead, and compare repeated observations under documented conditions.

question.prompt: What are two reasons a tiny operation might report zero elapsed time?

slides.title: A benchmark must make the intended work observable
keyPoints: Validate a result outside the timed interval
Do not discard the only output of the hot loop
Inspect implausible generated code rather than guessing
slides.narration: If a loop computes a result that the program never uses, an optimizing compiler may legally remove it. Timing the empty remainder does not measure the intended calculation. The source benchmark keeps a checksum and compares it with an independent formula after the timed interval. That verifies useful behavior without including verification time in that chosen boundary. Using volatile everywhere is not a general repair because it changes access semantics and may create a different workload. If a result looks implausibly fast, inspect the generated code, build options, input size, and timing boundary before announcing an optimization win.

slides.title: High utilization is not proof of useful progress
keyPoints: A spin loop can keep a core busy
A saturated dependency can leave other resources idle
Measure completions and wait time alongside utilization
slides.narration: A core at one hundred percent can be calculating useful results, spinning on a lock, or repeatedly handling irrelevant events. The utilization number alone cannot distinguish them. Likewise, low CPU use does not mean the service has spare end-to-end capacity: a serialized storage or network dependency may be saturated. Use utilization to guide a hypothesis, then connect it to completions, latency, and queue growth. If adding clients raises CPU use while throughput stays flat and latency rises, more admitted work may simply be increasing contention. The objective is useful completion under constraints, not the highest busy percentage.

slides.title: Control comparisons without hiding variation
keyPoints: Record compiler flags, input, and machine context
Alternate comparison order where practical
Report spread and uncertainty instead of one favorite run
slides.narration: Running version A once on a cool idle machine and B once after background work begins is a weak comparison. Repeat representative runs, record relevant conditions, and alternate ordering when practical to reduce drift. Variation can come from frequency changes, cache state, page faults, scheduling, contention, and instrumentation. Repetition reveals spread but does not automatically remove bias. If an apparent improvement is smaller than the experiment's noise, the evidence is weak. A statistically clear difference can still be operationally unimportant, so report both uncertainty and the size of the effect relevant to users.
